conventional_description: Motion sickness occurs when your brain receives conflicting signals from your inner ear, eyes, and body about whether you're moving. For example, reading in a car makes your eyes see a stationary page while your inner ear senses motion - this mismatch triggers nausea, dizziness, cold sweats, and sometimes vomiting. It's diagnosed based on your history and symptoms, and it can affect anyone, though some people are much more sensitive than others.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatments include over-the-counter antihistamines like dimenhydrinate (Dramamine) and meclizine, or prescription scopolamine patches worn behind the ear. Many people also rely on ginger supplements or acupressure wristbands. These approaches aim to block the nausea signal or calm the stomach, but they don't change the underlying tendency to get sick.
tcm_understanding:
TCM sees motion sickness as a sign that your internal environment is already unsettled. The Spleen is the organ most responsible for transforming food and fluids into usable Qi and Blood.
When the Spleen is weak - from poor diet, overwork, or constitutional tendency - it fails to manage fluids properly, and dampness builds up. Motion then acts like shaking a bottle of muddy water: the turbid dampness and phlegm rise upward, clouding your head and rebelling against your Stomach, causing that familiar wave of dizziness and nausea.
But dampness and phlegm are only part of the story. The Heart and Spleen work together to produce Blood, which nourishes the brain and anchors the spirit. When both are deficient, your brain is undernourished, and even gentle motion can feel overwhelming.
You might feel pale, exhausted, and lightheaded, with a fluttering heart. This pattern explains why some people get motion sickness even when they're not eating poorly - their Qi and Blood simply aren't enough to keep the head stable.
Kidney Essence provides the deepest foundation for balance and brain function. When this Essence is depleted - through aging, chronic illness, or overwork - the brain's mooring weakens, and chronic dizziness can be triggered by travel. This pattern often comes with lower back weakness, tinnitus, and poor memory. So while Western medicine sees one condition called motion sickness, TCM distinguishes at least four different patterns, each demanding its own herbal formula and acupuncture strategy.
classical_translation: "All wind with shaking and dizziness is attributed to the Liver. This establishes the link between internal wind and vertigo, a mechanism that can be triggered by motion sickness when Liver Yang or Liver Wind is stirred."
classical_source:

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking what the dizziness and nausea feel like and when they strike. If the sensation is a heavy, spinning vertigo that comes on quickly with movement and is accompanied by a thick, greasy feeling in the mouth and chest, the root is likely phlegm-dampness clogging the middle burner. The tongue coating will be thick and greasy, and the pulse will feel slippery, confirming that turbid phlegm is rebelling upward.
When the dizziness is milder but constant, and the person looks pale, tires easily, and may feel their heart flutter, the practitioner suspects the heart and spleen are not producing enough qi and blood to nourish the brain. Here the tongue is pale with a thin coating, and the pulse is weak and thready. The key clue is that symptoms worsen after exertion and improve with rest, pointing to a deficiency rather than an obstruction.
If the person has always been prone to motion sickness, with a history of bloating, loose stools, and heavy limbs, the pattern is spleen deficiency with dampness. The tongue appears pale and puffy with a greasy coating, and the pulse feels soft or weak. This constitutional weakness allows dampness to accumulate internally, so even slight motion triggers nausea and dizziness because the spleen cannot manage fluids properly.
In older adults or those with chronic depletion, kidney essence deficiency may be the root. The dizziness is often accompanied by tinnitus, a weak lower back, and frequent urination. The tongue is pale and thin with little coating, and the pulse is deep and fine. Because the kidneys fail to fill the marrow and support the brain, motion sickness becomes one part of a broader picture of declining vitality.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dizziness with a heavy, foggy sensation in the head", "Nausea and queasiness worsened by movement", "Feeling of fullness and oppression in the chest and upper abdomen", "Greasy, sticky tongue coating", "Heaviness in the limbs and body", "Poor appetite and bland taste in the mouth"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, heavy, or sweet foods, Damp, humid weather, Overeating or large meals, Prolonged sitting or inactivity, Worry and overthinking
patterns.better_with: Sitting still with eyes closed, Fresh, dry air, Light, warm meals, Warm drinks and ginger tea, Gentle movement or exercise
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak and fails to transform fluids, dampness accumulates and congeals into phlegm. This sticky phlegm settles in the Middle Burner and, whenever the body is jostled, turbid phlegm rebels upward to cloud the head and disturb the Stomach, producing the hallmark dizziness and nausea of motion sickness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with scalloped edges and a thick white greasy coating that appears moist. Pulse: slippery (Hua) and often soggy (Ru) or moderate (Huan).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-dampness arises when a weak Spleen fails to transform fluids, and it is easily aggravated by heavy, greasy foods and damp environments that add more dampness. Light, warm meals and ginger tea support the Spleen’s transforming function and warm the Middle Burner, helping to dry dampness and settle rebellious Qi. Staying still reduces the physical jostling that drives turbid phlegm upward, while gentle movement after eating aids the Spleen’s function and prevents stagnation, making the body less reactive to motion.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat light, warm, cooked meals and avoid greasy, fried, dairy-rich, or sweet foods that create dampness. Sip ginger tea before and during travel to warm the middle and settle the stomach. Gentle daily movement like walking supports the Spleen and prevents stagnation, but avoid overeating at any single meal.

patterns.why_this_happens:
The Heart and Spleen work together to produce Qi and Blood, which nourish the brain and anchor the spirit. When both are deficient, the brain is undernourished and the spirit becomes unsettled, so even gentle motion easily triggers dizziness and nausea.
The Spleen's weakness leads to poor appetite, bloating, and loose stools, while the Heart's deficiency causes palpitations, anxiety, and insomnia. This combination leaves the body under-resourced and overly reactive to travel, making motion sickness a frequent complaint.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, tender body with teeth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: fine, weak, and possibly choppy.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: This pattern is rooted in a lack of Qi and Blood to nourish the brain and settle the spirit. Rest conserves Qi, and eating warm, nourishing meals helps the Spleen produce more. Stress, fatigue, and hunger further deplete Qi and Blood, making the person more vulnerable to motion. Cold foods weaken the Spleen, which is already struggling, leading to more dizziness and nausea.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat regular, warm, cooked meals to support the Spleen. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that tax digestion. Before travel, have a light snack rather than an empty stomach. Gentle exercise like walking or tai chi builds Qi gradually. Manage stress with relaxation techniques to prevent further depletion of Heart Blood.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak, it fails to transform and transport fluids properly, allowing internal Dampness to accumulate. When you add motion-like a car or boat-the already unsettled Qi gets thrown into chaos, and the turbid Dampness rises upward to disturb the head, triggering dizziness and nausea.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, white greasy coating, moist surface. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and slow (Huan), soft and weak at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and raw foods directly damage the Spleen’s ability to transform fluids, increasing internal dampness and making motion sickness worse. Warmth-both in food and on the abdomen-supports the Spleen’s function and helps transform dampness, while ginger specifically warms the middle and descends rebellious Qi to stop nausea. Light meals and rest conserve Qi, preventing the overload that triggers symptoms.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congee; avoid cold, raw, and greasy items that further weaken the Spleen. Sip ginger tea before and during travel to warm the middle and transform dampness. Eat small, light meals and avoid overeating. Keep the belly covered and stay in a well-ventilated space.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Kidneys store Essence, which produces marrow to fill the brain and keep the head stable. When Kidney Essence is insufficient, the brain's foundation is weak, leading to chronic dizziness, a heavy sensation, and a tendency to lose balance. During travel, the constant motion disturbs this already fragile state, causing vertigo, nausea, and a deep, hollow feeling in the head that is often accompanied by tinnitus and soreness in the lower back.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with little or no coating, possibly fine cracks. Pulse: fine, deep, and weak, especially at both Chi (rear) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Essence is the body's deepest reserve; rest and nutrient-dense foods help replenish it, while overwork and prolonged motion drain it further. When Essence is low, the brain loses its anchor, so any sustained movement triggers dizziness and nausea. Warmth and gentle activity support the Kidney's function without exhausting its reserves.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, frequent meals that include kidney-nourishing foods like black sesame, walnuts, goji berries, and bone broths. Avoid overwork, late nights, and excessive sexual activity, which deplete Essence. Gentle daily movement such as tai chi or walking helps circulate Qi without exhausting the Kidneys.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really prevent motion sickness?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture can both prevent and treat motion sickness. By regulating the flow of Qi in the Stomach and calming the spirit, it reduces the tendency to feel nauseated. Many people find that weekly sessions leading up to a trip, combined with acupressure on the Neiguan point during travel, significantly decreases their symptoms. The effect is most reliable when the pattern is correctly identified - for example, clearing phlegm-dampness or nourishing Blood.

faqs.question: Are there specific acupressure points I can use while traveling?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. The most famous point is Neiguan (PC-6), located about three finger-widths below the wrist crease on the inner forearm. Firm pressure here for a few minutes can calm nausea and anxiety. Zusanli (ST-36) below the knee is another great point for strengthening the Spleen and settling the Stomach. You can press these points yourself or use acupressure wristbands that target Neiguan.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with my Dramamine or scopolamine patch?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but you should inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor. Some herbs have mild sedative properties, so combining them with antihistamines might increase drowsiness. Your practitioner can adjust the formula to avoid any overlap. Never stop prescribed medication abruptly without medical advice, and always bring a full list of your medications to your TCM consultation.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for children with motion sickness?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be very gentle and effective for children. Pediatric acupuncture often uses very shallow needling or non-needle techniques like acupressure and pediatric tuina massage. Herbal formulas can be given in reduced dosages or as granules. Ginger tea is a safe, time-tested home remedy for kids. Always work with a practitioner experienced in treating children.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet to stop getting motion sickness?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a big role, especially if your pattern involves dampness or Spleen weakness. In general, you'll be advised to avoid greasy, fried, cold, and raw foods that burden the Spleen and create dampness. Warm, cooked meals, soups, and ginger tea are your allies. Reducing dairy and sweets can also make a noticeable difference. These changes help calm the internal environment so motion doesn't trigger such a strong reaction.

faqs.question: How long until I can travel without feeling sick?
faqs.answer: Many people feel improvement after just a few weeks of herbs and acupuncture, but complete resolution depends on your pattern. Excess patterns like phlegm-dampness often respond quickly - you might travel comfortably within a month. Deficiency patterns take longer to rebuild reserves, so plan for a few months of consistent treatment before a big trip. Even during treatment, using acupressure and dietary strategies can make travel much easier.

research.title: Acupressure relieves the symptoms of motion sickness and reduces abnormal gastric activity
research.description: This randomized controlled trial examined the effect of acupressure at the Neiguan (P6) point on motion sickness induced by a rotating optokinetic drum. Participants receiving acupressure reported significantly less nausea and showed fewer abnormal gastric myoelectric activity patterns compared to sham acupressure, supporting the use of P6 stimulation for motion sickness.
research.periodical: Stern RM, Jokerst MD, Muth ER, Hollis C. Acupressure relieves the symptoms of motion sickness and reduces abnormal gastric activity. Altern Ther Health Med. 2001;7(4):91-94.

research.title: Effects of ginger on motion sickness and gastric slow-wave dysrhythmias induced by circular vection
research.description: In this placebo-controlled study, healthy volunteers were exposed to a rotating drum to induce motion sickness. Pretreatment with ginger (1,000 mg) significantly reduced nausea, delayed the onset of motion sickness, and decreased tachygastric activity compared to placebo, demonstrating ginger's antiemetic properties relevant to motion sickness.
research.periodical: Lien HC, Sun WM, Chen YH, Kim H, Hasler WL, Owyang C. Effects of ginger on motion sickness and gastric slow-wave dysrhythmias induced by circular vection. Am J Physiol Gastrointest Liver Physiol. 2003;284(3):G481-G489.

research.title: Stimulation of the wrist acupuncture point PC6 for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting
research.description: This Cochrane systematic review evaluated the effectiveness of PC6 stimulation for preventing nausea and vomiting after surgery. While not specific to motion sickness, the review provides high-level evidence that PC6 acupressure modulates the vomiting reflex, a mechanism directly applicable to motion sickness. The review found PC6 stimulation to be as effective as antiemetic drugs with fewer side effects.
research.periodical: Lee A, Chan SKC, Fan LTY. Stimulation of the wrist acupuncture point PC6 for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015;(11):CD003281.
